readings.title: Why a town changed its bus information
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town council once believed that its bus timetable was clear because every stop displayed a list of arrival times. However, complaints continued, especially from passengers who were unfamiliar with the area. The council asked volunteers to travel to different destinations using only the information available at the stops. The volunteers discovered that a timetable could be correct and still be difficult to use. Some stops showed the time but not the direction of travel. Others used route names that appeared nowhere on the street signs.

The council did not immediately buy electronic screens. It first changed the printed notices. Each notice now begins with a simple map showing the direction of the route. The name of the next major stop appears beside each time, and a short explanation shows how to read departures on public holidays. A telephone number is printed in large type for passengers who need further help. The council also tested the new notices with people who had not helped design them.

During the trial, volunteers were asked to find a bus to the hospital and explain when they would arrive. Most could do so more quickly than before, though several people still confused two stops with similar names. The council changed those labels before printing the final version. It also left space on each notice for temporary changes caused by roadworks.

The project showed that providing information is different from making it useful. A larger budget might have produced attractive screens, but it would not necessarily have solved the basic problem of unclear directions. By watching real passengers complete an ordinary journey, the council learned which details needed to come first. The same method could later help improve notices for other local services.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：公共服务与信息设计

readings.title: A small study of shared lunch spaces
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
At a workplace with employees on different shifts, managers wanted to create a shared lunch area. They assumed that a single large room would help colleagues meet. Before changing the building, a group of employees recorded where they ate for two weeks and noted why they chose those places. The records challenged the original idea. Many people did want to talk, but they had only fifteen minutes between tasks. Walking to a distant room would use much of that time. Others needed a quiet place because they worked in noisy surroundings.

The group proposed three modest changes instead of one large project. Tables near the main corridor would help workers on short breaks. A smaller room would remain quiet for those who preferred it. A noticeboard would show when social lunches were planned, so joining one would be a choice rather than an expectation. The managers asked staff from each shift to comment on the proposal, including employees who were rarely present at daytime meetings.

After six weeks, the group asked staff about their experiences. The corridor tables were popular, but people reported that the nearby door let in cold air. The quiet room was valued, although its signs were unclear and some visitors entered by mistake. Managers moved the tables a short distance and improved the signs. The noticeboard attracted fewer users than expected, so a weekly message was added to the existing staff bulletin.

No arrangement made every break ideal. Yet the changes cost less than rebuilding a large room and could be adjusted when work patterns changed. The most useful discovery was not a particular furniture plan. It was that the workers' reasons for choosing a place mattered as much as the number of empty seats. Managers agreed to repeat the discussion when new shifts were introduced.

readings.title: When a museum invited local memories
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A local museum planned an exhibition about an old railway station. Its staff had photographs and official records, but these mostly described the building and its timetable. They wanted to learn how the station had shaped ordinary lives. Notices invited residents to share memories, tickets and letters. The museum made it clear that people could tell a story without giving away a treasured object. Some contributors preferred to speak privately rather than have their names displayed.

At first, the staff grouped the stories by year. Visitors found the order easy to follow, yet it hid connections among different lives. One woman remembered waiting for her father to return from work; another recalled selling fruit to travellers at the same platform. The museum reorganized part of the exhibition around activities such as working, waiting and meeting. Dates remained available for visitors who wanted them.

The staff also faced a question of accuracy. Two people remembered the station clock showing different times on the day of a major storm. Rather than choose one memory and present it as certain, the exhibition explained that personal recollections can differ. It placed the memories beside a newspaper report and asked visitors what each source could tell them. In this way, uncertainty became a chance to think about evidence.

When the exhibition opened, several visitors added details that the museum had missed, including the fact that a nearby shop lent umbrellas on rainy days. The staff recorded these comments and checked them before changing any labels. The project did more than add colourful stories to official records. It gave residents a way to see their own experience as part of a shared history, while showing that memories should be handled with care. A small table invited further written recollections throughout the exhibition.

readings.title: A garden that measured more than harvests
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When a neighbourhood group started a small garden, it expected to judge success by the amount of food produced. Volunteers planted vegetables in raised beds and weighed each harvest. The figures were useful, but they did not explain why some beds were cared for regularly while others were neglected. The group invited volunteers to describe their experiences. Several said they enjoyed the work but could not come at the same time every week. New members found the watering instructions confusing, and older members were unsure whom to ask when tools were missing.

The coordinators introduced a simple notebook beside the tool shed. Volunteers recorded what they had done and what still needed attention. They also arranged short introductions at different times of day, rather than expecting everyone to attend one Saturday meeting. A shared calendar allowed members to exchange tasks when work or family duties changed. None of these ideas required new land or expensive equipment.

At the end of the season, the group compared harvest records with participation notes. The total weight of vegetables had risen only a little. However, more people had taken part, and fewer plants had been lost during hot weeks. Members had also learned which crops were suitable for the limited shade. Some residents valued the garden chiefly as a place to meet neighbours, while others cared more about fresh food.

The group decided to keep measuring harvests, but not to use weight as its only measure. It would also ask whether volunteers could join without difficulty and whether the garden was learning from mistakes. A project can produce a modest harvest yet still create valuable skills and relationships. Measuring several outcomes helped the group make a more honest decision about what to improve next. The records also made it easier to explain those choices to neighbours.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A clear public notice does more than present correct facts. It helps readers decide what to do next. Before publishing a new notice, staff should ask people who have not seen the plan to use it for a real task. Their questions may reveal missing directions or words that are familiar only to the writers. Such feedback is not a sign that the first draft has failed. It is information that can make the final version more useful. When a service changes, the notice should also explain where people can find current details. A simple map, a date, and a contact number may save many visitors an unnecessary journey.
translation.explanation: 注意more than、who引导的定语从句及may表示的可能性。
translation.referenceAnswer: 清楚的公共告示不只是呈现正确事实，还能帮助读者决定下一步做什么。发布新告示前，工作人员应请没见过方案的人利用告示完成一项真实任务。他们提出的问题可能暴露缺失的指引，或只有撰写者才熟悉的用词。这类反馈并不意味着初稿失败，而是能让最终版本更实用的信息。服务发生变化时，告示还应说明人们从哪里获取最新详情。一张简单的地图、一个日期和一个联系电话，可能使许多访客免于白跑一趟。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a community centre suggesting how it could make course information easier for new learners to use. Describe two changes and explain how the centre could check whether they help.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖信息集中呈现、路线图与真实用户测试三个要点。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Centre Manager,
I am writing to suggest two changes to the information about your evening courses. First, each course page could show the building, room number, start date and total cost together. New learners would then be able to plan their visit without searching several pages. Second, the centre could provide a simple map from the nearest bus stop to the correct entrance. This would be especially helpful for people arriving after dark.
To check whether these changes work, please ask a few people who have never attended a course to find a room using only the new information. Staff could record the questions they ask and the time they need. After the first month, a short survey could identify anything that is still unclear. These small steps would make joining a course easier.
Yours sincerely,
A learner
